Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

decimal (development version)

Known issues

  • Combining decimal Arrow columns of different scales or storage widths can silently misread values: 3.125 can come back as 31.25. This affects arrow::concat_arrays(), arrow::concat_tables() and arrow::open_dataset() over parts written separately, followed by collect() or arrange(), because arrow compares this package’s extension types by name alone. Until this is fixed, pin one type with arrow_decimal_type() for every part that will be appended or combined (#37).

Bug fixes

  • as.double() and casts to double are now correctly rounded. They went through R’s internal string parser, which can be off by one unit in the last place (decimal("83E25"), decimal("1e23", scale = 15)), returned Inf for 1.7976931348623158E+308 instead of the largest double, and gave NaN or Inf once a value had more than about 4932 digits, as any value in a vector with scale = 5000 does. Each result is now checked exactly against the midpoints to its neighbouring doubles, so it no longer depends on the platform’s C library, and the conversion is tested against nearly 4,000 values computed by Python (#45).

  • decimal() and as_decimal() now refuse a value whose scale, its fractional digits minus its exponent, lies outside integer range, such as "1E-2147483650", instead of storing it with the wrong scale. A value whose exponent alone is out of range but whose scale is not, such as "1.5e+2147483648", is now accepted (#52).

  • adjusted() now raises its “out of integer range” error for an adjusted exponent of -2147483648 instead of returning NA (#54).

  • The native routines now check the type and length of every context argument and raise an error for a malformed one, instead of crashing R when called directly through .Call() with a zero-length vector (#41).

  • Converting an Arrow column whose chunks carry different decimal storage now checks every chunk. Chunks that differ only in precision, such as dataset parts whose values had different magnitudes, now combine exactly, where arrow used to fail with “Array chunks must all be same type”. Chunks that differ in scale or width raise an error of class decimal_arrow_chunk_error instead of being misread (#37).

  • The bundled ‘mpdecimal’ now builds for WebAssembly (webR). Its configuration did not recognise the wasm32 target and stopped with “unsupported platform”.

  • floor(), ceiling(), trunc(), round() and signif() now return infinities and quiet NaNs unchanged, payload included, and raise no signal, as base R and Python’s Decimal.to_integral_value() do (#49). signif() turned them into NA, and the others trapped invalid_operation. A signaling NaN still raises invalid_operation. A quantize() trap on a special value no longer suggests raising the context precision.

  • mean() on a decimal vector now honours trim, which it silently ignored (#53). It drops floor(n * trim) values from each end of the sorted vector, as mean.default() does, and returns the median once trim reaches 0.5.

  • is.unsorted() now compares decimal values, honouring strictly and na.rm, instead of the stored text, which made is.unsorted(decimal(c("9", "10"))) TRUE (#47). The “Decimal values” vignette now notes that merge() orders its result by a decimal key’s text (#57).

  • pmax() and pmin() now refuse a decimal argument whose scale is finer than the first argument’s (#48). Base R gives the result the first argument’s attributes, so pmax(decimal(c("10", "9")), decimal("9.5")) returned values held at one decimal place under a scale of zero. Bring the arguments to a common scale first, as in pmax(as_decimal(x, scale = 1), y), or put the finest-scaled argument first. These functions are not generic, so with a non-decimal first argument they still return a character vector: write pmax(x, 2L) or pmax(as_decimal(2L), x) rather than pmax(2L, x).

  • New ?decimal-summaries documents sum(), prod(), mean(), min(), max() and range() for decimal vectors, including a limit no method can lift (#42): R picks the method from the first argument alone, so when that is not a decimal, min(), max() and range() compare the stored text and return a character vector (min(10L, decimal("9")) is "10"), and sum() and prod() fail. Put a decimal first, min(x, 10L), or convert the first argument, min(as_decimal(10L), x).

  • options(decimal.default_scale = ) no longer leaks into the package’s own conversions (#43). It is the default scale for decimal() and as_decimal() on character, integer and double input, but integer operands, rounding quantums, counts and constants picked it up too. Under default_scale = 2, round(x, 3) and quantize(x, "0.001") returned two digits and x * 3L gained two extra; under default_scale = -2, x + 150L added 200, x * 3L gave 0, mean(x) trapped division_by_zero and summary() reported no missing values; under default_scale = 0, summary() quartiles were wrong. Integers and character operands now convert exactly at the scale their value gives.

  • as_decimal() on a decimal vector without scale now returns it unchanged, rather than rescaling it to decimal.default_scale. Arrow decimal arrays likewise keep the scale of their Arrow type under that option, in as_decimal(), arrow_as_data_frame(), as.data.frame() and arrow::read_parquet(); before, with default_scale = 1, 1.25 and 2.75 read back as 1.2 and 2.8 (#43).

  • summary() quartiles no longer depend on options(digits), OutDec, scipen or the numeric locale (#44). The interpolation weight was built by formatting a double, so options(digits = 1) gave a 1st quartile of 1.8 for c(1, 2, 4, 7.1) instead of 1.75, and OutDec = "," raised an error. The weight is now chosen from exact text.

  • vctrs::vec_sort(), vctrs::vec_order(), dplyr::arrange(.locale = ) and tidyr::expand() now order negative decimals by value in every collation locale (#46). Under en_US.UTF-8, vec_sort(decimal(c("-1.25", "-1.2"))) gave -1.20 before -1.25, because the order proxy was text that sorted correctly only byte by byte. It is now an integer rank. sort(), order(), rank() and dplyr::arrange() without .locale were already correct.

  • x[[i]] <- value now widens x to the scale of a finer value, as x[i] <- value always did, instead of silently rounding: y[[2]] <- decimal("9.123") on a scale-2 y used to store 9.12 (#50).

  • Behaviour change: vctrs::vec_cast() from a decimal to a coarser decimal type is now a lossy cast. When rounding would change a value it raises an error of class vctrs_error_cast_lossy, which vctrs::allow_lossy_cast() turns back into rounding; before, vec_cast(decimal("1.55"), decimal("1.0")) silently gave 1.6. Dropping trailing zeros, NA and special values still casts. This reaches functions that cast a replacement to an existing column: tidyr::replace_na(decimal(c(NA, "1.5")), decimal("0.125")) now errors rather than filling in 0.1. Combining vectors of different scales (c(), vec_c(), rbind(), dplyr::bind_rows(), dplyr::if_else(), dplyr::coalesce()) still takes the finer scale, and as_decimal(x, scale = ) still rounds on request (#50).

  • Behaviour change: vctrs::vec_cast() from character to a decimal type now uses that type’s scale (#51). vec_c("1.123", "2", .ptype = decimal("1.0")) used to return a vector labelled scale 1 that stored “1.123” and “2” unchanged. Text with fewer digits is padded exactly; text that would be rounded is a lossy cast, as for a coarser decimal, so vec_cast("1.23", decimal()) now errors. decimal() and as_decimal() still infer the scale from the text.

  • arrow::as_arrow_array() now refuses a value wider than a pinned decimal type with an error of class decimal_arrow_precision_error, naming the digits the value needs and the type’s precision. Arrow’s own cast silently wrapped a value too wide for the type’s integer width: 39 nines pinned to decimal128(38, 0) became a negative number, and 2^128 + 7 pinned to decimal128(5, 0) became 7 (#38).

  • A decimal vector with a negative scale is now written to Arrow at storage scale 0, which Parquet accepts and which holds the same values exactly; it reads back with scale 0, not its original negative scale. Before, arrow::write_parquet() and arrow::write_dataset() rejected the column only after opening the destination, emptying an existing file or leaving a 0-byte part. arrow_decimal_type() now validates its arguments and refuses a scale above the precision, which Parquet rejects the same way. A table that already holds such a field can still empty the destination file, because arrow opens it before checking; this is documented in ?decimal_arrow (#39).

  • Documented that negative zero loses its sign through Arrow: an Arrow decimal has a single zero, so -0.00 reads back as 0.00 (#40).

decimal 0.1.1

CRAN release: 2026-09-23

  • decimal vectors now convert to and from ‘Arrow’ decimal arrays directly. as_decimal() gained methods for Array and ChunkedArray. An Arrow decimal column of any width converts exactly, taking its scale from the Arrow type: Arrow’s own decimal-to-string cast produces this package’s canonical storage form once the exponent letter is folded to lowercase, so the strings need no re-parsing, and a property test guards that invariant. For 1,000,000 decimal128() values that takes 0.27s against 0.78s for casting to string and calling decimal(). Arrow integer columns convert exactly at every width, including int64 and uint64 values a double cannot hold. Other Arrow types convert through the ordinary as_decimal() rules for the equivalent R vector.

  • A decimal column now becomes an Arrow decimal field in arrow::arrow_table(), arrow::write_parquet() and arrow::write_dataset(). The field is an Arrow extension type whose storage is a real decimal128() or decimal256(), so Spark, DuckDB, pandas and other readers see a plain decimal column, while in R it returns as a decimal vector on every read path: as.data.frame(), arrow::read_parquet() and dplyr::collect() included. New arrow_decimal_type() pins a precision and scale for a column that will be appended to. Infinities and NaNs, which no Arrow decimal can represent, now raise an error on conversion instead of round-tripping through the ‘vctrs’ extension type; keep such a column as a string if you need them.

  • Arrow’s compute engine does not operate on extension columns. For arrow-side arithmetic or filtering on a decimal column, write a plain field by passing a plain Arrow decimal type to arrow::as_arrow_array() or by setting options(decimal.arrow_extension = FALSE). A plain field comes back from arrow’s own conversion as a double wearing the decimal class, because arrow reapplies the column’s recorded R attributes; format() and as.character() now refuse such an object rather than print rounded values. New arrow_as_data_frame() converts an Arrow Table or RecordBatch to a data frame, reading plain decimal fields, including those in files written by other systems, as decimal vectors, and leaving every other column to arrow.

  • Fixed memory leaks on the error paths of the native kernels. An R error raised while an mpd_t was allocated abandoned it, because R’s error handling unwinds past the code that would have freed it. Parsing an invalid decimal string leaked every handle the operation held, and an allocation failure part-way through setting up an operation leaked the handles already allocated. An R allocation failure while storing a result string leaked the formatted text too; that text is now released under R_UnwindProtect().

  • summary() now works on decimal vectors. It reports the same six statistics as [summary.default()] plus an NA's count, computed in decimal arithmetic and returned as a decimal vector, so figures that a double would round are preserved. Quartiles use the type 7 definition, matching stats::quantile().

  • Fixed is.na(), is.nan(), is.infinite(), is_qnan() and is_snan() returning malformed logical vectors. They forwarded mpdecimal’s flag bits – 4 for NaN, 8 for sNaN, 2 for Infinity – instead of TRUE. The results printed correctly and compared equal with ==, but which() found no matching elements, sum() over-counted, and identical() was false against the obvious expectation.

  • DESCRIPTION now declares URL and BugReports, so the CRAN page links to the source repository and the issue tracker.

  • Building a decimal vector from character is substantially faster. The fractional-digit scan that decimal() performs on every element moved from R to C, which for 100,000 values takes construction from 1.13s to 0.05s when scale is supplied (about 22x) and from 2.28s to 0.05s when it is inferred (about 45x). Inferring the scale now costs the same as supplying it. This matters most when loading decimal data from ‘Arrow’ or a database, where the values arrive as a character vector in one call.

  • New vignette vignette("arrow-decimal-types"), covering lossless conversion between decimal vectors and Arrow’s decimal128() / decimal256() types in both directions, including chunked arrays, Parquet columns, and the cases Arrow decimals cannot represent.

  • format() on a decimal vector now accepts the extra arguments that table printers pass to every column, such as digits, na.encode and justify from format.data.frame(), timezone from ‘data.table’ and trim from knitr::kable(), so decimal columns print inside a base data.frame, a data.table and a kable() table. The arguments are ignored rather than honored, so an exact value is never silently rounded for display. Arguments that would change how a number is written, such as nsmall, scientific and big.mark, are an error.

  • Fixed rbind() on data frames with decimal columns, which always failed with “Can’t assign to elements past the end”. Assigning past the end of a decimal vector now grows it with missing values, as it does a base vector, and binding columns of different scales takes the finer one. x[] <- value now replaces every element instead of failing.

  • match(), %in% and base merge() now compare decimal values rather than their stored text, so 2.5 matches 2.50, as == already said. Whole numbers still match integers and strings: decimal("20") %in% 20L stays TRUE.

  • New section in vignette("decimal-values") on decimal columns in a ‘data.table’: what works, and workarounds for the operations data.table runs on the stored text instead of the values, such as sorting and grouped min() and max().
